item.title: Jinny Lu, the World’s Ugliest Dog, Proves That Looks Aren’t Everything
item.description:
Ugly is subjective. But in this competition, it means everything.

Year after year, owners enter their pets in a contest to become the one, the only, world’s ugliest dog.

It may not sound like a badge of honor, but for the pets and their owners, this competition is proof that where you come from does not define where you end up.

If you can make it here, you can truly make it anywhere.

With her floppy tongue and bulging eyes, this year’s winner, Jinny Lu, a 6-year-old pug, did not disappoint.

Jinny Lu was the runner-up in 2025. This was her fourth attempt to win the top prize.

According to her biography, Jinny Lu was “found in a wooden box in freezing weather in the mountains of South Korea.”

She likes to sneak “onto kitchen chairs and very stealthily puts her amazing tongue into everyone’s food bowls,” according to her biography.

She also likes to spend time snuggling, sunbathing and greeting visitors.

Her fun fact? She screams at her reflection in the mirror.

The World’s Ugliest Dog Contest, which takes place during the Sonoma County Fair at the Sonoma County Fairgrounds in Santa Rosa, Calif., celebrated its 50th year on Friday.

The contest promotes dog adoptions and celebrates “the imperfections that make all dogs special and unique.”

The dogs are treated as stars as they strut along a red carpet lined by adoring fans.

Judges consider the pet’s background and story. Previous winners include dogs who “embody resilience and inspiration.”

Jinny Lu won $5,000, a trophy and a trip to New York for a live appearance on the “Today” show, which is scheduled for Monday.

Jinny Lu, who emerged as the winner from among eight contestants, will also appear on limited-edition cans of Mug Root Beer, a sponsor of the competition.

Pinky, an albino Pomeranian Chihuahua mix with a rosy snout, was the runner-up and took home $3,000 and a trophy.

Otto, a Chihuahua mix with a cleft palate, won third place, earning $2,000 and a trophy.

And if you just can’t get enough, here are the winners from past years:

In 2025, Petunia, a hairless English-French bulldog mix from Eugene, Ore., was crowned the winner.

In 2024 there was Wild Thang, a wide-eyed, tongue-flopping mop of long fur. In 2023, there was Scooter, who also let his tongue hang loose and whose hind legs were reversed. And in 2022, there was Mr. Happy Face, a Chihuahua mix.

The contest was suspended in 2020 and 2021 because of the Covid-19 pandemic. In 2019, the champion was Scamp the Tramp.

Once a year, dogs, their owners, and fans gather at the Sonoma County Fair for the World's Ugliest Dog Contest. 'Ugly' takes on a whole different meaning here. I couldn't pick a favorite if I tried.

item.title: Nazi Jokes and Vulgar Insults: The Edgy Gun Influencer Embraced by the G.O.P.
item.description:
Standing in a San Antonio barbecue joint, the speaker of the House, Mike Johnson, laid out a stark contrast between two congressional candidates in a sprawling West Texas border district. Voters could choose the “common sense” of the G.O.P. nominee, Brandon Herrera, he said, or the “crazy” positions of his Democratic opponent.

Until recently, however, establishment Republicans were trying to paint Mr. Herrera as the crazy one.

A self-described gun-rights absolutist and YouTuber known for his inflammatory humor, Mr. Herrera, 30, was initially opposed this year by both Mr. Johnson and President Trump as he challenged the district’s Republican incumbent, Tony Gonzales, for a second straight time. Mr. Gonzales and his allies spent millions painting Mr. Herrera as extreme, highlighting old videos in which he made wildly offensive jokes like saying that a Nazi-era submachine gun was “the original ghetto blaster” and “Hitler’s street sweeper.”

But after a sexual misconduct scandal forced Mr. Gonzales out of the race and then out of Congress this year, top Republicans quickly closed ranks around Mr. Herrera.

In an era where candidates’ online pasts are etched into the public record, Mr. Herrera’s rise is testing voters’ tolerance for comments, even those made in jest, that are beyond the pale of public acceptability.

It also underscores the anti-establishment energy coursing through both parties. As they wrestle for control of Congress, national leaders have jumped into shotgun marriages with outsider candidates — and those candidates, in turn, are welcoming help from an establishment they once attacked.

“After a brutal primary on all sides,” Mr. Herrera told reporters in San Antonio late last month, “the focus has to be bringing the party together.”

The district leans Republican — Mr. Trump carried it by 15 percentage points in 2024 — but Democrats believe Mr. Herrera’s polarizing nature could give their nominee, Katy Padilla Stout, a chance.

Mr. Herrera says he does not need to moderate, but since 2024, he has sought to broaden his appeal. That year, he ran largely on a pro-gun platform in the district, which hugs a long stretch of border and reaches from San Antonio to El Paso — and which includes Uvalde, the site of a school shooting in 2022 that killed 19 children and two teachers. This year, he has crisscrossed the district to host town halls on veterans’ benefits, water scarcity and guardrails for data centers.

His digital footprint continues to dog him. In the days before Mr. Johnson rallied for Mr. Herrera and held a fund-raiser for him, a video resurfaced of the YouTuber using crude, sexualized insults against a female gun-control activist in 2022.

But Mr. Herrera says that the voters he meets are far more concerned about gas and grocery costs than about his online archive.

“The only people who have ever cared about that are either in the media or in D.C.,” he said in an interview with The New York Times, adding, “As long as I can convince voters that I’m right on the issues, then I shouldn’t have any problem winning their vote in November.”

The comments by Mr. Herrera in the latest unearthed video are graphic and, Democrats hope, the kind of thing that could keep some Republican voters home in November.

In the video from July 2022, Mr. Herrera used crude language to insult Shannon Watts, who founded the gun-control group Moms Demand Action after the Sandy Hook massacre in 2012.

Ms. Padilla Stout has sought to highlight the remarks. At a recent gathering of left-leaning women in the northern hills of San Antonio, she paused to ask if children were out of earshot before recounting what he had said.

“That is not the type of person you want making decisions for you and your children,” she said.

In the interview, Mr. Herrera waved off the comments as part of the comedic persona he assumes as a YouTuber. While he wouldn’t use the same language as a political candidate, he said, he’s not apologizing.

“I know the difference between the way that you speak in a comedy performance, so to speak, and the way that you speak in a political environment,” he said, adding: “I’ve always toed that line perfectly fine. What they’re going to do is they’re going to pretend jokes are policy, and they’re going to purposely pretend that they don’t know the difference.”

Ms. Padilla Stout has also pointed to a video of Mr. Herrera highlighting his ownership of a 1939 English edition of “Mein Kampf,” and has circulated clips of him joking about Nazi atrocities against Jews.

In the interview, Mr. Herrera vehemently denied that he was antisemitic, and said he owned an annotated copy of “Mein Kampf” as part of a historical book collection.

Yehuda Remer, a Second Amendment activist who has known Mr. Herrera for a decade and is Orthodox Jewish, said the idea that Mr. Herrera was a Nazi was preposterous.

“If Brandon was actually antisemitic, he wouldn’t have helped me along my journey, and continued to help me,” Mr. Remer said.

Originally from North Carolina, Mr. Herrera built up a base of more than four million subscribers with gun reviews, weapon tests and re-enactments of famous assassinations. He also created The AK Guy, a company that restores historical firearms, and other businesses. He moved to San Antonio in 2020.

The provocative humor that fueled his career also threatened his political rise.

During his Republican primary in 2024, the Republican Jewish Coalition, a pro-Israel group, spent millions to amplify an old joke by Mr. Herrera that made light of veterans who die by suicide.

“Fools like Brandon Herrera who mock veterans do not belong in Congress or Texas,” a narrator said in the ad.

(In an interview, he called the idea that he does not support veterans “a disingenuous lie,” and pointed to fund-raisers that he and his podcast co-hosts have held for veterans’ causes.)

Mr. Herrera has positioned himself as a conservative Republican, earning endorsements from members of the right-wing House Freedom Caucus.

He opposes aid to all foreign countries, including Israel, “while the U.S. is still in debt.” He is against all new restrictions on firearms, including red flag laws. He would also “like to see deportations ramp up a good bit, with a priority toward convicted criminals.”

While he is closely aligned with Mr. Trump, he has broken from the administration at times. He has lobbied against the federal government’s plans to build a border wall in Big Bend National Park.

Mr. Herrera has won the support of some previously skeptical Republicans, including Greg Brockhouse, a Republican consultant in San Antonio who worked on Mr. Gonzales’s campaigns.

Mr. Herrera is “much calmer than the online presence, much more thoughtful,” Mr. Brockhouse said in an interview. But he, along with some other Republicans, worries that Mr. Herrera has not done enough to court moderate voters.

“This ain’t a walk,” Mr. Brockhouse said. “And if anybody in Brandon Herrera’s team thinks it’s a walk, they’re going to lose.”

Ms. Padilla Stout said she decided to run to stop a gun influencer from representing Uvalde.

She has staked out center-left positions on immigration and public safety, despite Speaker Johnson’s claim that she supported “open borders” and abolishing prisons. Her family hunts and owns guns, she said, but she backs age and mental health checks.

House Democrats’ campaign arm, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, recently added the district to its midterm target list, saying Mr. Herrera’s “disturbing history of extremism” had put it in play. Democrats also argue that the decision by Gov. Greg Abbott, a Republican, not to replace Mr. Gonzales — which has left the district unrepresented since April — signals Republican worries about keeping the seat.

“Why wouldn’t you call a special election?” Ms. Padilla Stout said at the July campaign event. “Because you’re scared you’re going to lose.” A spokesman for Mr. Abbott declined to comment on the governor’s reasoning.

But the campaign arm hasn’t yet put its money where its mouth is.

“I’m, like, in the most toxic relationship of my life” with the D.C.C.C., Ms. Padilla Stout, 41, said at the July campaign event. “I find myself thinking, ‘I don’t want your time and attention. I want your money!’”

The national party may have bigger fish to fry. Republican-led redistricting in Texas put Democrats on the defensive in three districts held by the party.

Some moderate Republicans who are on the fence about Ms. Padilla Stout say she appears to be to the left of what the district wants, while Mr. Herrera may be too far to the right.

Amy Posada, who was a congressional staff member for Mr. Gonzales from 2021 to 2022, said that if Ms. Padilla Stout could show her that she would work with Republicans, and hear out conservative voters, “she’s got my vote.”

What interested me most about Herrera is how he seeks to defy conventional political wisdom with a strategy similar to President Trump. Addressing past comments he's been strongly criticized for, Herrera told me, "These are not statements said by people who are aspiring to run for office." To him, that's a strength, not a weakness, because it only reinforces his credentials as an outsider.

item.title: A Free-for-All in Alaska as 17 Candidates Compete to Be Governor
item.description:
By the time the last candidate for governor rolled through the 74th annual Golden Days parade in Fairbanks, Alaska, late last month, even the master of ceremonies sounded exhausted.

Along with the antique cars, taekwondo students and saloon girls, he had introduced eight campaigns for governor — not even half the candidates on the Aug. 18 primary ballot. As the parade neared its end, marchers came by promoting a measure in November to repeal the state’s open primary and ranked-choice voting system.

“Well,” the announcer quipped, “at least if that passes, our next parade will be shorter.”

On Tuesday, voters will pick four of 17 candidates to advance to the November general election for governor at a critical juncture for the oil-rich, cash-poor state. Several forces are coming together to make this a weird political moment: Alaska’s open primary system, which places Democrats, Republicans and independents on a single ballot; the first governor’s race in nearly a quarter century without an incumbent or an heir apparent; and a growing consensus that the state faces some of its biggest decisions since the Trans-Alaska Pipeline was built five decades ago.

With so many choices, “it’s like eating a salad — you have to really dig in and take your time to get to the good parts,” said Nick Stepovich, a former legislator, son of a former governor and owner of a downtown Fairbanks saloon. “And there’s always this risk that it’s a bad meal.”

The campaign is also unfolding in the shadow of one of the nation’s marquee Senate races, which pits the Republican incumbent, Dan Sullivan, against a former representative, Mary Peltola, the last Democrat to win statewide office in Alaska. That race is drawing tens of millions of dollars in outside spending, driving up advertising costs and consuming much of the state’s limited television and radio inventory.

The math has scrambled the usual assumptions about party politics in this Republican state. Political observers and even other candidates expect both Democrats, Tom Begich and Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, to advance to November.

“You’ve got 80,000 voters on the left, and 110,000 on the right or the middle-right,” said Art Hackney, a longtime Republican consultant. The two Democrats get to split those 80,000, he said, while a dozen or so Republicans fight for the slightly larger pot on the right.

With polls showing the top finisher may win less than 25 percent of the vote, the difference between advancing or going home could be a few hundred, or a few dozen, ballots.

Taking no vote taken for granted, Mr. Kreiss-Tomkins rode a skiff 450 miles down the Yukon River in July and had driven a snowmobile to the Arctic Ocean earlier in the year. Republican Adam Crum tried “guerrilla campaigning,” skipping traditional political events to serve hot chocolate in the spring to hundreds of snowmobilers in the woods.

“You go wherever there might be voters,” said Mr. Begich, a former Democratic legislator and singer-songwriter whose Democratic father, Nick Begich Sr., served in the House, whose Republican nephew, Nick Begich III, serves there now, and whose brother, Mark Begich, was a senator.

Nearly every candidate also agrees on something else: Alaska has reached an inflection point. Despite its vast oil wealth, the state’s unique fiscal model — no statewide income or sales tax and annual checks to each resident from Alaska’s oil fund — has left lawmakers scrambling to keep schools open, pave roads and stop population loss.

“We are the richest poor state you could possibly imagine,” said Mr. Crum, a former state revenue and health commissioner.

Mr. Kreiss-Tomkins, who started his political career at age 13 directing the state campaign of Vermont’s governor-turned-presidential hopeful Howard Dean, said the next governor and legislature “will be making decisions that will shape the state for the next half century.”

The state’s votes have favored President Trump in three consecutive presidential elections, but the legislature has been governed for nearly a decade by a coalition of Democrats, Republicans and independents. They’ve largely sidestepped culture-war fights to focus on Alaska’s fiscal and environmental challenges.

Still, the state government is now frozen. The outgoing governor, Mike Dunleavy, a Republican who polls among the least popular governors in the country, has repeatedly vetoed efforts to increase education funding and restructure the budget. In turn, the legislature has rejected the governor’s efforts to cap state spending and increase dividend payments from the state oil fund.

“We all think the state needs change,” said Click Bishop, a candidate for governor and former Republican legislator who has been labeled a “Republican in name only” by others in the race because of his willingness to work with Democrats. “Nobody is exactly happy with how things are going; we just disagree on the solution.”

The field includes a former governor, Bill Walker, who shocked the political establishment with his surprise late entry; a podiatrist and political novice, Matt Heilala, who has already spent more than $1.4 million of his own money; and five Republicans aligned with Mr. Trump and trying to win the conservative base.

Sophia Huff, a voter at the Fairbanks parade, said that with so many choices, “it’s hard to know where to start.”

She had brought her two young children to the parade, and she said she’s not sure if she’ll have the attention span to vote. So far no candidate has prioritized the only issue that matters to her: how to convince toddlers to sleep through the night.

With just days to go, no one is sure what will happen, said University of Alaska Anchorage political scientist Forrest Nabors.

Planned Parenthood Alliance Advocates of Alaska, the health organization’s political arm, endorsed Mr. Begich in the primary because the crowded nature of the race gave its support more weight. The political arm of Alaska’s largest teachers union, the NEA-Alaska, endorsed three candidates — Mr. Begich, Mr. Kreiss-Tomkins and Mr. Bishop — to give options to education-minded voters.

After the primary, candidates who qualify for the general election have until Aug. 31 to decide whether to remain on the ballot. In November, voters will use ranked-choice voting to pick the next governor from the final four.

Mr. Begich and Mr. Kreiss-Tomkins said they have already begun talking about what happens if they both qualify: Do they work as a coalition, or does one drop out? Each said he wants to make sure a progressive wins.

Bernadette Wilson, a conservative media personality who has led the Republican field in recent polls, wants fellow Republicans to rally behind one candidate if several advance to November. The goal, she said, is to send a Republican to Juneau “with the strongest possible mandate.”

So far none have agreed.

All of the Republicans would love an endorsement from Mr. Trump, although he has not yet shown any inclination to get involved. Ms. Wilson noted that she’s the only candidate who held a fund-raiser at Mar-a-Lago.

She also helped organize the November ballot measure to repeal Alaska’s open primaries and ranked-choice voting system. She says the cluttered primary proves the current system is too confusing.

Others in the race find the breadth of choices refreshing.

“I honor the system we have,” said Mr. Walker, the former governor running as an independent. He jumped in late because, he said, no one else was talking about the hard choices facing Alaska. “It’s unprecedented. It’s history-making. It’s also very liberating.”

item.title: Years of Trump Support Came Undone in 15 Minutes in an Airport.
item.description:
Brent Jindra, a tech salesman, voted for President Trump three times, drawn by his aggressive immigration agenda. He never imagined the crackdown would ensnare his own wife.

Last month, moments after the couple got off their flight in Burbank, Calif., a young man in a brown hooded sweatshirt stopped Galina Bobreneva.

“Congratulations, you’ve been chosen for secondary screening,” he told her, according to the couple’s recollection.

The man was a federal agent, and after questioning Ms. Bobreneva for about 15 minutes, he led her away in handcuffs to an unmarked vehicle.

“I’m only doing my job,” he said. “Everything will be OK.”

So began a 16-day ordeal: a night on the floor of a basement holding cell in downtown Los Angeles; two weeks in a Mojave Desert detention center and a frantic legal effort to win her release.

Freed on a $35,000 bond with an electronic monitor clamped to her ankle, she is now fighting to stay in the United States against federal charges of overstaying her visa.

Ms. Bobreneva, who is from Russia, has a pending green card application, and her lawyer asserts that she was never out of lawful status.

Her case represents a new front in President Trump’s mass deportation drive: arrests at airports of people whose visas have expired but who have active immigration cases and no criminal history.

Although green-card applicants with expired visas can be detained under federal law, previous administrations did not consider them to be in the country unlawfully. But as the Trump administration seeks to nearly double its daily arrests to 2,000 people, it is detaining and attempting to deport thousands of people who believed they were following the rules.

“The allure of the MAGA campaign was around illegal entries of criminals,” said Mr. Jindra, 48. “There was never a mandate for this president to turn the barrel of the gun and start going after people who legally entered.”

In response to questions about Ms. Bobreneva’s case, the Department of Homeland Security said in a statement that she was “an illegal alien” targeted for arrest because “she overstayed her welcome in violation of our nation’s laws.”

“To be clear, work authorization or a pending application do NOT confer legal status in the United States,” the agency said in a statement.

Mr. Trump’s immigration agenda, which helped propel him to the White House for a second term, is becoming a vulnerability for the Republican Party ahead of the midterms as even some members of his base have begun condemning ICE’s hard-line tactics.

Mr. Jindra considered himself a MAGA patriot until his wife’s detention.

“She did not jump a wall, she did not swim a river,” he said. “She came in Trump’s beautiful, big front door.”

Ms. Bobreneva arrived on a tourist visa in late 2021, extended it twice following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and applied for asylum in 2022. She met Mr. Jindra in March 2025 and by December they were married.

“It was your storybook romance,” he said.

Mr. Jindra petitioned in April to sponsor his wife for a marriage-based green card. They received official confirmation the application had been accepted. She was fingerprinted.

The newlyweds bought a “dream house” in Cleveland, Ohio, where Mr. Jindra was raised, and intended to relocate there soon.

They planned a trip to Sonoma County’s wine country to celebrate Ms. Bobreneva’s 40th birthday on July 16. Mr. Jindra booked a suite at a boutique hotel, prepaid for visits to three vineyards and hired a driver.

They never made it.

On July 13, the couple boarded a flight from San Francisco to Burbank, where Mr. Jindra planned to meet clients and Ms. Bobreneva to see friends.

Approached by plainclothes agents at the airport, the couple first thought it was a ruse.

“When the ICE badge was flipped, you could tell that was legit,” recalled Mr. Jindra, referring to Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

He immediately called their immigration lawyer, but the agents refused to speak with him. They ushered Ms. Bobreneva into a room, leaving her husband on the concourse, flanked by Burbank airport police, he said.

Inside, the agents told Ms. Bobreneva that she had overstayed her visa. “I was absolutely sure this was a mistake,” she said.

She explained that she was in the process of securing a green card and presented documents.

When an agent pulled out handcuffs, Ms. Bobreneva was stunned. She asked to give her engagement ring and other jewelry to her husband. They then led her away, saying that Mr. Jindra would know where to find her.

“A U.S. citizen just watched his wife get dragged away and had no idea where she’s going,” recalled Mr. Jindra.

The white S.U.V. sped off into the darkness. Ms. Bobreneva, alone with two men, said she feared for her safety until they arrived at an ICE facility.

She was held in a frigid room with a handful of women. She recalled a gaunt diabetic immigrant in her 70s pleading for insulin, to no avail. Ms. Bobreneva curled up on the ground under a foil blanket.

About 18 hours later, she was shackled at the ankles, waist and wrists and loaded into an unmarked van with several other immigrants. They bounced up and down in the sweltering vehicle as it raced toward the detention center in Adelanto.

“I felt like a piece of meat, not like a human,” recalled Ms. Bobreneva.

By the time she changed into blue prison garb and was assigned bunk L63 — a lower bed in the women’s section — it was 5 a.m. Thirty minutes later, as she drifted off to sleep, orders blared over the loudspeaker for detainee count and breakfast lineup.

Sleep deprivation was a constant, she said. Lights were always on. Hand-held radios carried by the guards crackled day and night. On her birthday, Ms. Bobreneva recalled, she shared chocolate she had ordered from the commissary with fellow Russian-speaking detainees from Russia, Ukraine, Belarus and Armenia.

Ms. Bobreneva described neglect, filth and people in despair.

For 120 women, there were seven showers; only four worked. Potable water was scarce; ailing people were denied care until they required hospitalization, she said, echoing allegations in a federal lawsuit.

The GEO Group, which operates the detention center, declined to comment on Ms. Bobreneva’s allegations and referred questions to ICE.

In a statement, a homeland security spokesperson said: “Any claim that there are subprime conditions at Adelanto ICE processing facility are FALSE. All detainees are provided with proper meals, water, medical treatment, and have opportunities to communicate with their family members and lawyers.”

ICE did not respond to questions.

“You become a number,” she said. “Nobody cares. There is zero empathy.”

Mr. Jindra visited when allowed, three times a week, and scrambled to secure her release.

Two weeks passed.

Their lawyer, Patrick Valdez, requested a bond hearing, scheduled for July 28. Ms. Bobreneva was released July 29 on a $35,000 bond with an ankle monitor and an order to report to ICE in San Francisco Aug. 5.

Over dinner at a seafood restaurant in Redwood City the night before her appointment, Ms. Bobreneva barely touched her crab cakes. She had been struggling to sleep and was terrified of being detained again.

“I never thought that it was so easy to take freedom from anyone,” she said.

Mr. Jindra, too, was nervous.

“We are living in fear in my own country,” he said.

Early the next morning, they joined a line outside the immigration building that wrapped around the block. Ms. Bobreneva entered with her lawyer more than two hours later.

They emerged with instructions from ICE to report back on Sept. 7.

The couple returned to Redwood City, where unopened birthday gifts and deflating balloons sat on their dining room table, alongside a vase of two dozen wilted roses.

“I cannot celebrate anything,” Ms. Bobreneva said.

Her first court appearance is Oct. 22, but her case will take months to be resolved.

Wearing the electronic monitor, Ms. Bobreneva is confined to a tight perimeter.

Last Sunday, the couple ventured to the beach.

Ms. Bobreneva was “enjoying her freedom,” Mr. Jindra said, “all 75-mile radius of it.”

Kirsten Noyes contributed research.

item.title: Democrats Face a Potential Tea Party Moment
item.description:
A movement of young, progressive outsiders has stormed Democratic politics this year, sparking a wave of contentious primary contests across the country and fueling a fraught debate over whether these new, left-wing candidates are remaking the party in their image.

But as primary season winds to a close, the results reveal not only the strength but also the potential limitations of this insurgent movement.

In Minnesota last week, Peggy Flanagan, the lieutenant governor, won a Senate primary by a double-digit margin, pressing a fiercely progressive message to defeat a more moderate opponent. Just a week earlier, Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, a left-leaning Democrat, won a Senate primary in Michigan despite being vastly outspent. And Francesca Hong, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, came close to winning a primary for governor in Wisconsin, falling short by less than one percentage point.

The results marked a new level of political strength for candidates affiliated with a resurgent, activist left, showing that their movement can be competitive in statewide primaries, well beyond deep-blue House districts.

Yet while a vocal group of strategists, activists and college-educated voters have raced to embrace these pugnacious, boldly liberal — and in some cases untested — candidates, some of the voters who have historically been most crucial to the party’s fortunes remain skeptical.

In Michigan and Wisconsin, both pivotal battleground states, the progressive candidates appeared to have struggled to sway voters who have long been the backbone of the party — including Black, more moderate and older Americans who vote reliably.

As left-wing candidates have notched victories in primary after primary, many progressives hope they will be able to move the Democratic Party further to the left — mirroring, in some ways, how the rise of the Tea Party movement nearly two decades ago pushed the Republican Party much further to the right. But the results raise questions about whether these candidates can piece together a broad enough coalition of Democrats, independents and moderates to win general elections in swing states that could determine whether Democrats are able to regain power in Congress and, eventually, the White House.

“Would I put a D.S.A. member up for governor in New York or Massachusetts?” said Chris Walton, the former chairman of the Democratic Party of Milwaukee County. “Sure, we can take a chance. But it makes it harder in a state like Wisconsin, where you’re starting out at the 48-yard line and have to figure out how to get to 50.”

The next major tests for the left will come this fall in a smattering of battleground House districts, and as Dr. El-Sayed and Troy Jackson, a progressive former state senator in Maine, fight to win seats that Democrats need to capture control of the Senate.

The primary results indicate that to win, some of those nominees must not only persuade independent voters, but also shore up their own bases.

In Michigan, Dr. El-Sayed trailed in majority-Black townships across the state. While he was popular with younger voters, there were signs that he was weaker than his Democratic primary opponent, Representative Haley Stevens, among older voters, who vote more reliably.

In Wisconsin, Ms. Hong, who had been the heavy favorite in polling, lost her primary to David Crowley, the Milwaukee County executive who would be the state’s first Black governor, in a shock upset. Mr. Crowley had an edge in metro Milwaukee and in rural counties, while Ms. Hong showed strength in smaller cities and suburbs, as well as counties that are home to college towns.

Senator Bernie Sanders, the Vermont independent who championed progressive candidates across the country including Dr. El-Sayed and Ms. Flanagan, said he is confident that Democrats, as well as independents, will rally behind the nominees in the fall.

“If our candidates keep talking about the issues that are relevant to ordinary people — the issues of affordability, the issues of health care, the issues of education, housing, basic necessities of life, protecting Social Security — against Republicans who want to cut Social Security, you know what?” said Mr. Sanders. “Our guys are gonna win, and they’ll win big.”

But even in some of the most heavily Democratic neighborhoods in America, there are signs of fissures. In New York, Black and Latino leaders have expressed alarm over democratic socialist victories in gentrifying neighborhoods, worrying that the day-to-day concerns of longtime residents will be overlooked.

Representative Adriano Espaillat, a New York Democrat and chair of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus, lost his primary earlier this summer to a far-left challenger, Darializa Avila Chevalier, a democratic socialist who had voiced support for abolishing the police, borders and prisons and seizing property from landlords.

In an interview, he nodded to precinct-level data showing that while his opponent did better in whiter, younger, and higher-income areas, he was strong across many older and majority-Hispanic areas.

“They claim to have the agenda of the working class, but that’s not what the people in those communities feel,” Mr. Espaillat said. “Those neighborhoods, I believe, are concerned about affordability, but they’re also concerned about public safety. You know, they’re also concerned about the types of issues that D.S.A. may have a different position on than they do.”

The growth of a new insurgent left was supercharged by the Democrats’ loss in the 2024 presidential race, which created a fresh opening for a new kind of politician who could channel Democratic anger with what they saw as a sclerotic party establishment.

The following year, Zohran Mamdani — fueled by an activist, progressive left that was animated by the Palestinian cause and fury toward billionaires — won a surprise victory in the New York City race for mayor, prompting a new class of Democratic candidates to embrace a similar bold vision.

The candidates share some unifying principles: Support for “Medicare for all,” opposition to A.I. data centers, a commitment to ending corporate money in politics and a view that opposition to American support for Israel is a moral litmus test, fueled by a belief that the Gaza war amounted to a genocide.

But beneath that broad platform, there are real differences among the candidates.

“There is a wide range of candidates who have been able to position themselves as either progressive or populist or even under the D.S.A.,” said Matt Barreto, a Democratic pollster who worked with former President Joseph R. Biden Jr.’s campaign. “It’s way looser ideologically than people think.”

Ms. Hong, a state lawmaker, is a member of the D.S.A., which is not officially part of the Democratic Party.

Dr. El-Sayed, who calls himself a “capitalist,” is not a D.S.A. member, nor was he endorsed by the group. He does have a yearslong relationship with the organization, speaking at several local events during the first Trump administration.

And in Minnesota, Ms. Flanagan eagerly embraced progressive policies and allies like Mr. Sanders but is a lifetime member of the Democratic-Farmer-Labor Party, the Democratic Party’s engine in the state, which endorsed her bid.

Ms. Flanagan, who defeated Representative Angie Craig by 20 percentage points, said she focused on organizing support in every corner of her home state.

“The coalition that we have built is faith, labor, young people, folks in greater Minnesota, farmers,” she said in an interview. “When you build relationships with people, even if you don’t see eye to eye on everything, I think that’s the way that we won this election.”

Still, despite the differences, all three races illustrated how Democratic views of what makes a candidate electable have shifted — within some limits.

In both Minnesota and Michigan, voters rejected an argument made by Democratic leaders that the more moderate candidates — Ms. Craig and Ms. Stevens — were better positioned to win statewide.

But in Wisconsin, Ms. Hong’s baggage from pandemic-era statements that she struggled to explain — including one in which she suggested canceling Thanksgiving and another describing her young biracial son as offering her “proximity to whiteness” — appeared to be too much for voters.

“People are less willing to trust the political class and what we think is electable,” said Lauren Hitt, a Democratic strategist who has worked for candidates across the ideological spectrum. “They’re looking for people who break the mold, but if you break the mold so much that you’re eccentric, that’s not the solution either.”

Charles Franklin, the director of the Marquette Law School poll in Wisconsin, said that since the rise of Mr. Mamdani, it has been “maybe easy to be caught up in just how strong democratic socialists were doing.”

But now, he added, “when you go to statewide races with that more heterogeneous electorate, I think you’re seeing some limits on that, even within Democratic primaries.”

Ruth Igielnik contributed reporting.

item.title: AIPAC Targets Progressive Democrat in Race to Replace Swalwell
item.description:
The sleepy suburbs east of San Francisco have suddenly become the latest battleground in the ideological fight over the future of the Democratic Party.

Super PACs, including two with ties to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, have flooded the region with millions of dollars in advertising ahead of a special election on Tuesday to determine who will replace Eric Swalwell in Congress for the next few months.

In California’s 14th congressional district, Aisha Wahab, a progressive Democratic state senator, is facing off against Melissa Hernandez, a moderate Democrat who sits on the Bay Area Rapid Transit board. The two Democrats are vying to fill out the remainder of Mr. Swalwell’s term after he resigned abruptly in April amid allegations of sexual misconduct as he was running for California governor.

Ms. Wahab seemed to be the clear front-runner after she emerged from the June primary with 43 percent of the vote compared to 17 percent for Ms. Hernandez.

But the sudden influx of cash, not just from AIPAC but also from another super PAC created to counter the group, has turned the race into an unexpected brawl between the establishment and progressive wings of the Democratic Party. It comes just two weeks after Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive Democrat, narrowly won the Senate primary in Michigan in the face of AIPAC’s hefty support for his moderate opponent.

Neither Ms. Wahab nor Ms. Hernandez has made Middle East politics a focus of their campaigns.

But in recent weeks Ms. Wahab has found herself fending off $2.9 million in attacks from outside groups, much of it coming from the United Democracy Project, AIPAC’s main super PAC. The group has also spent more than $825,000 supporting Ms. Hernandez.

Ms. Wahab, 39, is the first Afghan American and Muslim elected to the California State Senate. During a candidate forum in April, Ms. Wahab said “yes” when a moderator asked if she considered “what is happening to the Palestinian people a genocide.”

Ms. Hernandez, 51, responded by saying that she believed Israel had the right to defend itself after the Hamas attacks on Oct. 7, 2023. “However,” she said, “the destruction in Gaza has gone too far.”

Like the candidates, the super PACs have not focused on Israel in their advertising in the race.

Instead, one ad funded by the AIPAC super PAC accused Ms. Wahab of watering down legislation that sought to stiffen penalties against child sex predators. Ms. Wahab responded that she had helped make it “illegal and a felony to traffic or solicit minors.”

Another super PAC called Bold America, which has received some funding from AIPAC’s group, has spent $2.4 million supporting Ms. Hernandez and opposing Ms. Wahab.

Patrick Dorton, a spokesman for AIPAC’s super PAC, did not return a call seeking comment.

American Priorities, a super PAC created to counter pro-Israel spending, put $200,000 into supporting Ms. Wahab. “Don’t buy the Republican AIPAC lies,” says an ad from the group, which has backed left-wing critics of Israel in congressional primaries in New York. Ms. Wahab has also received support from J Street Action Fund, a liberal Jewish organization.

AIPAC has become such a polarizing player in Democratic politics that drawing attention to its spending in the race could help Ms. Wahab in her heavily Democratic district in Northern California, said Noah Finneburgh, a Democratic political consultant in the East Bay who is not involved with either candidate.

“I definitely think that those attacks could backfire,” he said.

In total, groups have spent $4.9 million on television and digital advertising in the run-up to Tuesday’s special election, according to the ad tracking firm AdImpact. Even more has been spent on mailers, text messages and phone calls, campaign finance disclosures show.

The two candidates did not return calls seeking interviews.

Both candidates have filed complaints with the Federal Election Commission. Ms. Wahab has asked regulators to investigate a rash of social media posts that she claimed made false statements about her and may have been spread by fake bot accounts. Ms. Hernandez alleged that Ms. Wahab unlawfully transferred money from her state-level campaign account through a county Democratic committee to hide corporate donations.

Ms. Wahab was endorsed by the California Democratic Party and has support from several labor unions and Our Revolution, the left-wing group founded by Senator Bernie Sanders. The group, with which Mr. Sanders is no longer involved, said it planned to fan out across the East Bay this weekend to support Ms. Wahab.

Both candidates have emphasized a desire to work in Washington on lowering costs for Americans. Ms. Wahab has said she wants to “end pointless wars” that cost tax dollars and drive up consumer prices. Ms. Hernandez has said she would prioritize small businesses and pledged to bring “fiscal discipline” to Washington.

The winner of Tuesday’s election will serve the remainder of Mr. Swalwell’s term, which ends in January. Ms. Wahab and Ms. Hernandez will face off again in November for the two-year term that begins that same month.

item.title: In ‘The Brink of War,’ a Return to an Era of Razor-Edge Diplomacy
item.description:
It was, as one person in the room described it, something of an Agatha Christie thriller, if Agatha Christie had written about superpower summits.

There were the leaders of the two nuclear giants huddled in a supposedly haunted house built on top of lava along a windswept coast, with rain lashing the windows and the fate of the world at stake.

The arms control meeting in Reykjavik, Iceland, between Ronald Reagan and Mikhail S. Gorbachev in 1986 has slipped into the fog of history. But the tense, unscripted encounter that was deemed a failure at the time arguably proved to be the beginning of the end of the Cold War.

Now 40 years later, Hollywood has embarked on a mission to rescue Reykjavik from obscurity with a star-studded movie, “The Brink of War,” featuring Jeff Daniels as Mr. Reagan, Jared Harris as Mr. Gorbachev and J.K. Simmons as Secretary of State George P. Shultz. The film, out this weekend, serves as a kind of bookend to the 2023 hit “Oppenheimer,” taking the nuclear arms race born in the remote desert of Los Alamos to its crescendo in the Arctic frontier of Iceland.

“Like any great story, there was a lot at stake,” Mr. Daniels said in a joint interview with Mr. Harris last week. “It was life or death. There were 70,000 nuclear weapons pointed at each other, and nothing to stop them, and that whole mutual assured destruction was not even a deterrent. It was the end of the world.”

Mr. Harris, a British actor, recalled that it felt even more real at the time growing up in Europe. “We were aware that we were on a knife’s edge,” he said. “We were on the front doorstep of any nuclear exchange.”

This is not just history, in the eyes of the filmmakers, but a parable for the current day as well. As wars rage and the world’s superpowers appear headed once again for an arms race, the film is a reminder that in an age of polarization even vast divisions can be bridged.

Somehow, the world’s most famous cold warrior, the man who had condemned the Soviet Union as an “evil empire” that would be left on “the ash heap of history,” found himself in a room with the leader of international communism. And the two agreed that it was time to step back from the precipice of planetary destruction.

“You don’t know if you’re going to find common ground or not until you do,” said Michael Russell Gunn, who wrote the film and made his feature film directorial debut. “I want to encourage people to have courage to talk to one another.”

Mr. Gunn’s movie seeks to make two days of talking into a gripping drama. The film revolves almost entirely around these two leaders, presenting them as fully realized flesh-and-blood figures struggling to overcome profound differences during a weekend at Hofdi House in Reykjavik.

There was, indeed, something cinematic about the real-life Reykjavik meeting. Unlike nearly every other presidential summit, the two leaders sat down without a set agenda and without a pre-agreed outcome. Dispensing with talking points and entourages, they spent more than 10 hours together over the weekend of Oct. 11-12, 1986, talking, arguing, cajoling, needling, haggling and even dreaming. At one point, Mr. Reagan and Mr. Gorbachev decided the United States and the Soviet Union should give up their nuclear weapons — all of them.

“The Brink of War” was shot in Iceland, in the house used for the 1986 summit, with Mr. Daniels, Mr. Harris and Mr. Simmons sitting at the same modest walnut table in the same modest room where Mr. Reagan, Mr. Gorbachev and Mr. Shultz sat along with Eduard Shevardnadze, the Soviet foreign minister.

Mr. Daniels made a point of visiting the house the day before shooting started and just sitting there for a couple hours going over lines and absorbing the history. “You can feel it,” he said. “There’s a presence.”

Mr. Gunn received an alarmed call telling him that Mr. Daniels was at the house. “I get this frantic call from the gaffer,” Mr. Gunn recalled. “‘Jeff’s here! He’s in the chair, like in the dark in the room!’ And I was like, ‘Leave! Get out of there! Leave him be!’ And he was just there to like soak it in.”

By legend, Hofdi House, built in 1909, is haunted by the ghosts either of Viking warriors or a woman who died there called “the White Lady.” The British ambassador in the 1950s was spooked enough to force his ministry to sell the property. Mr. Harris said he never saw any spirits, but joked, “I think the ghost stole my beanie hat, which you know you need in Iceland.”

The White Lady’s accommodations were so small that the C.I.A. and K.G.B. officers who accompanied the leaders quarreled over who got the better bathroom, negotiators drafted documents while sitting on plywood on top of a bathtub and a Reagan aide had to crouch on the floor next to the president’s knees during a staff meeting in a secure room. U.S. and Soviet military officers carrying the two nuclear footballs, which could be used to launch world-ending strikes, stood at attention near each other outside the negotiating room.

Mr. Daniels’s Reagan is not the “Saturday Night Live” version, but a serious figure, at once idealistic yet stubborn, mindful of his brush with death at the hands of a would-be assassin five years earlier and determined to use his additional lease on life to end the nightmare of nuclear Armageddon.

To that end, the moviemakers did not press the physical likeness too much. “We could have put plastic cheekbones,” Mr. Daniels said. “We could have redone my whole face with plastics.” But, he added, “you push the audience away, so that’s what they see are all the externals.”

Instead, he said, he focused on Mr. Reagan’s voice and mannerisms, the cocking of the head. “I had a hook for me, which got me into it, which was the way he said the word, ‘well,’” he said, adopting Mr. Reagan’s husky voice for a moment. “You land that, it’s like a hook in a fish.”

Until the 1986 meeting, the history of arms control talks between the United States and the Soviet Union had all been about slowing the growth of their mutual nuclear arsenals. But there in that whiteboard house on the edge of nowhere the American president and Soviet general secretary decided for the first time to actually reduce the number of nuclear weapons in the world. And they got so excited at one point that they agreed to abolish all of their nuclear weapons.

The unexpected grand bargain fell apart at the last minute over Mr. Gorbachev’s insistence that Mr. Reagan give up plans to try to build a nuclear shield in the form of a missile defense system called the Strategic Defense Initiative, or S.D.I. in the jargon of the day or “Star Wars” to the skeptics. Reagan refused and the two men took leave of each other angry and disappointed.

But what seemed like a letdown changed the course of history and set their two countries on a path toward the destruction of tens of thousands of nuclear warheads. Barely a year later, Mr. Reagan and Mr. Gorbachev signed the first agreement eliminating a whole category of nuclear weapons, the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty, or I.N.F., which led to subsequent pacts negotiated or ratified by George H.W. Bush, Bill Clinton, George W. Bush and Barack Obama bringing down nuclear stockpiles even further.

“It started a precipitous decline in nuclear weapons,” Ken Adelman, who served as the director of the U.S. Arms Control and Disarmament Agency and had to sit at Mr. Reagan’s knees at Reykjavik, said in an interview.

When Mr. Reagan and Mr. Gorbachev met, the Soviet Union had more than 40,000 nuclear warheads and the United States more than 23,000, according to the Federation of American Scientists. Russia now has about 4,400 and the United States about 3,700, or collectively about 13 percent of the Reykjavik-era totals.

Today, however, the world appears heading in a different direction. President Trump withdrew from the I.N.F. treaty in 2019, citing Russian cheating, and the New Start treaty signed by Mr. Obama, the last legal limit on the size of the nuclear arsenals, lapsed in February. While Mr. Trump has talked about brokering a new three-way treaty with both Russia and China, he has done little to actually pursue it.

Mr. Adelman, who chronicled the summit in his 2014 book “Reagan at Reykjavik” and issued a revised version this summer adopting the film’s name, “The Brink of War,” said Mr. Gunn’s film captured “the tension in the room.”

The improvisational approach the two leaders took, he recalled, stunned everyone. “It was going to be a come-as-you-are, a grip-and-grin summit,” Mr. Adelman said. “We were shocked out of our minds that Gorbachev was ready to roll. He wanted something done.”

As for Mr. Reagan, Mr. Adelman said, he too proved something. “What was surprising to me at Reykjavik was how antinuclear Reagan was,” he said. “I didn’t know that. We were mocking the ban-the-bomb guys. We were sneering at them.” And it turned out that, in his own way, Mr. Reagan was one of them.

Mr. Adelman said that while Mr. Reagan’s original S.D.I. vision was fantasy at the time and still has not yet emerged all these decades later, he paved the way for a future focused on defensive weapons, which in recent years have shown their worth in missile systems like Israel’s Iron Dome and America’s Patriots.

Mr. Gunn said he became interested in telling the story of Reykjavik when he was introduced to Mr. Shultz at Stanford’s Hoover Institution. He ultimately dedicated the movie to the former secretary of state, who died at 100 in 2021. “He said even he didn’t truly believe that the Soviet Union could end,” Mr. Gunn said. “It was only Reagan that had this kind of leap of imagination.”

Mr. Daniels said he hopes the film will inspire others to make a similar leap. “I would like to think that the leaders of the world today would have the courage to do what these two guys tried to do back in 1986,” he said. “Get into a room and figure out how to make us a safer world for all of us.”

item.title: Blanche Refuses to Say He’ll Always Be Independent of Trump as Attorney General
item.description:
Todd Blanche, the newly confirmed attorney general, refused to say on Sunday that he would always act independently of White House control but claimed during an interview that President Trump has “never” demanded he prosecute specific people.

Mr. Blanche, displaying a greater ease in fielding a variety of pointed questions than his predecessor, Pam Bondi, sought to balance his loyalty to the president and a commitment to the evenhanded administration of justice during an appearance on NBC’s “Meet the Press.”

“There’s a big difference between saying we will always do our job and investigate any case, and act independently of the White House,” Mr. Blanche said when pressed to pledge his independence by the show’s host, Kristen Welker.

“No, I’m not going to pledge that, and no attorney general should ever pledge that,” he said.

But he suggested in another interview that he was not afraid to push back. “It’s my job to talk to him about those issues, which I have done for many years and I will continue to do,” he said on “Fox News Sunday.”

Mr. Blanche told NBC that Mr. Trump had never asked him to do anything illegal or unethical — and claimed that reports of White House meddling in the department were overhyped.

“There is this extraordinarily false narrative that the president wakes up in the morning and calls me and says, ‘Todd, go prosecute X or Y,’” Mr. Blanche said. “He does not do that. He has never done that. He will never do that.”

In September, Mr. Trump demanded the immediate prosecution of several adversaries in a social media post aimed at Ms. Bondi. He fired Ms. Bondi in April, in part because he thought she was moving too slowly in prosecuting his perceived enemies whom he had identified, with scant or nonexistent evidence, as being criminals.

Mr. Blanche, then her deputy, was elevated to fill the post and was narrowly confirmed by the Senate earlier this month. His confirmation was imperiled by the opposition of some Republicans who questioned his role in a $1.8 billion compensation fund for purported victims of abuses by the Biden-era Justice Department and a deal granting Mr. Trump sweeping immunity from tax investigations.

After weeks of wrangling, Mr. Blanche secured the support of several holdouts by putting on paper a commitment to rescinding his previous order creating the fund and limiting the scope of the tax immunity agreement.

On Sunday, he repeated his claim that the fund was dead but said that those who felt they had been wronged — including Capitol rioters convicted of crimes and pardoned by Mr. Trump — could still apply for compensation through the courts.

On Friday, Mr. Blanche, a former federal prosecutor who served as Mr. Trump’s lead criminal defense lawyer, appeared alongside the president at an event in Long Island with Bruce Blakeman, the Nassau County executive running for governor of New York.

“In my Department of Justice, if anybody touches a federal law enforcement officer in any way inappropriate, we will prosecute them to the fullest extent of the law,” Mr. Blanche said at the event.

When Ms. Welker asked him to square that statement with Mr. Trump’s mass clemency to the rioters on the first day of his second term, Mr. Blanche offered the same answer he gave during his confirmation hearing: Presidents have the constitutional right to pardon anyone they want.

He also expressed support for Jeanine Pirro, the U.S. attorney in Washington who has drawn Mr. Trump’s wrath over her dropping of charges against a man accused of vandalizing the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and blaming a “botched” renovation.

Mr. Blanche’s public support was a significant endorsement for Ms. Pirro, a longtime friend and ally of Mr. Trump, who has recently become a target.

“I absolutely support U.S. Attorney Pirro, as does President Trump,” he said — even though Mr. Trump has considered firing her and raged against her decision.

“Now, that’s different than whether the president is extraordinarily frustrated at what happened in that case, and I don’t in any way fault him for that,” added Mr. Blanche, who suggested the department was still investigating vandalism in and around the pool.

Mr. Blanche emphasized his commitment to focusing on law and order during a speech at Justice Department headquarters last week, seeking to shift the narrative away from the political maelstrom that has engulfed the department during his tenure.

Mr. Trump, he told Fox News, “wants law enforcement out there arresting bad guys.”

item.title: Indiana Prepares for More Rain After Days of Deadly Storms
item.description:
Recovery efforts were underway on Sunday in Indiana as portions of the state prepared for extreme heat, more rain and potential flooding after days of storms.

Stubborn storm systems have drenched the Midwest since Tuesday and have caused at least seven deaths in Indiana and displaced scores of residents. More than 50 counties have been affected.

Rushing water inundated homes, submerged roadways and flooded shopping centers. In Indianapolis, the state capital, the White River jumped its banks and threatened portions of the city.

Emergency responders have had to perform rescues by boat.

Wind gusts reached around 100 miles per hour in some areas, according to Gov. Mike Braun, and peak flows broke a 113-year-old record for water height, according to the U.S. Geological Survey.

“This is about as widespread of a weather issue we’ve had in years,” Mr. Braun said at a news briefing on Saturday.

President Trump on Saturday approved the governor’s emergency declaration, allowing disaster assistance from the Federal Emergency Management Agency to flow to 53 Indiana counties.

Indiana’s Department of Homeland Security confirmed that there had been seven fatalities caused by the storms. One victim’s age was not released, while the others ranged from 4 to 86.

The State Emergency Operations Center did not know how many residents had been displaced but said more than 200 people were in shelters across Indiana.

In Noblesville, a city of 75,000 people north of Indianapolis, more than 500 homes had been affected by record floodwaters, according to Mayor Chris Jensen. About 170 residents and their pets were evacuated.

Mayor Scott Fadness of Fishers, Ind., said on Sunday that water rescues had been conducted in the area since Thursday. On Saturday, he said emergency personnel had rescued about a dozen individuals and their pets by the White River.

“At this point, our rescue operations have concluded and we now turn our attention to recovery, “ he said on Sunday.

In Portage, Ind., one person died in an apparent home explosion. Storm damage on the roads slowed emergency workers, according to officials.

In Geneva, Ind., a 4-year-old boy died after a tree fell on his home, the Jennings County Sheriff’s Office said.

In Delaware County, a teenager died after entering a river during flooding on Wednesday, according to the sheriff’s office.

The storms have pelted Ohio, Kentucky and Illinois with persistent rain and flooding. One person suffered a weather-related death in Ohio, according to officials.

Recovery efforts are underway as floodwaters are expected to recede in some areas of Indiana, but warnings remain in effect.

In southwestern Indiana, the heat index was expected to reach 105 degrees on Sunday, bringing more dangerous weather to the state.

Inclement weather is forecast throughout the region. Thunderstorms are expected across large swaths of the Ohio Valley, Central Appalachians and Mid-Atlantic. The repeated storms raise the risk of flash flooding. Farther east in West Virginia, two rounds of storms could result in flash floods.

Josh Ryan, a Carmel, Ind., resident with a background in heating, cooling and plumbing, has offered to pump water from flooded homes for free to help residents begin the recovery process, which he characterized as predatory.

“I’m not a government official. I don’t have millions of dollars,” he said in an interview, “But one thing I can do is help people get started.”

Nazaneen Ghaffar, Jacey Fortin and J. David Goodman contributed reporting.

item.title: Top Admiral Praises Sailors but Concedes Hardships After Visit to U.S.S. Lincoln
item.description:
Service at sea “for long periods isn’t for everyone,” the head of United States Central Command said on Sunday, after visiting the beleaguered U.S.S. Abraham Lincoln, the latest American aircraft carrier to report poor living conditions and poor morale after months in the Middle East.

The Lincoln, a San Diego-based carrier with a crew of about 5,000 sailors, is supporting U.S. operations in the Middle East against Iran. Democratic lawmakers have cited reports of shortages of basic supplies, water contamination, plumbing issues and deteriorating mental health aboard the carrier, which has been deployed for almost nine months.

But Admiral Brad Cooper insisted in a statement posted on social media post that “the Lincoln currently has among the lowest number of cases related to mental health” among the Navy’s 11 active aircraft carriers.

“That doesn’t mean that all is perfect,” Admiral Cooper acknowledged a day after his visit to the carrier. He said that a long deployment at sea “is uniquely challenging and tough, and every single one of us, including me, reacts to stressors in different ways.”

The admiral’s comments differed from those of his boss, President Trump, who on Friday dismissed concerns about difficult conditions reported aboard the ship. Asked whether he was concerned about the crew’s mental health and whether he thought the deployment had gone on too long, the president said: “No. No. No.”

He added: “Not nearly long enough.”

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth also dismissed reports last week about the grim conditions aboard the U.S.S. Lincoln, saying the situation had been “misrepresented.”

Still, the Navy is sending the aircraft carrier George Washington to relieve the Lincoln, according to a U.S. official who spoke on the condition of anonymity. The official was not authorized to speak publicly about ship schedules.

Admiral Cooper’s comments are in line with previous Pentagon officers in past administrations. Gen. Colin Powell, the former chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, often maintained that the first priority of senior leaders is to look after the safety and health of their troops.

“They will never let you down as long as you never let them down,” Mr. Powell wrote in his book, “It Worked For Me: In Life And Leadership.”

item.title: Trump Orders Pentagon to Curtail Military Exercises With Ally South Korea
item.description:
President Trump said on Sunday that he had instructed the Pentagon to reduce joint military exercises with South Korea, a longtime U.S. ally and a linchpin of America’s national security strategy in the Asia-Pacific region.

The announcement may heighten growing worries among Asian allies over what the United States is now willing to do to deter China, given the enormous distraction and resource drain of the U.S.-Israel war against Iran. The United States is running low on critical weapons and has been moving military resources out of Asia to the Middle East.

In a convoluted social media post, Mr. Trump complained that Seoul did not “join us in the Denuclearization of the Islamic Republic of Iran.” In the same post, he said that North Korea under Kim Jong Un had been “unthreatening and respectful” while he has been president.

In his post Mr. Trump did not mention a rift in relations in 2017, when the North Korean leader called him a “mentally deranged dotard” after Mr. Trump delivered a speech at the U.N. threatening to “totally destroy” North Korea if the United States had to defend itself or its allies.

Now Mr. Trump is speaking only of what he on Sunday called his “very good relationship” with North Korea and its leader. In his post, he said that because of those ties, he was “not happy with the fact that the United States has, long ago, agreed to participate in Joint Military exercises with South Korea.”

“These exercises are not only costly, with much of these costs paid for by the United States of America (as usual!), but send a signal that is totally inappropriate and hostile, to a Country that, as long as Donald J. Trump has been President, has been unthreatening and respectful,” Mr. Trump said in his post.

Mr. Trump said that because it was too late to cancel the exercises entirely, he had asked Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to “substantially reduce” U.S. participation.

The U.S. and South Korean militaries have held joint exercises for more than 70 years, since 1955, after the 1953 armistice that ended the Korean War.It was unclear just how the Pentagon would scale back its role in the joint military exercises, called Ulchi Freedom Shield, which are set to begin on Monday and run for 11 days.

The exercises are held most summers with South Korea’s armed forces and with other U.S. allies in the Asia-Pacific region. North Korea has always decried the exercises as dress rehearsals for an invasion.

The exercises focus on how the allied militaries can counter a wide range of security threats, including drones and cyberattacks, while also strengthening combined defenses. They are designed to help U.S. allies defend against threats from North Korea.

The Pentagon was taken aback by Mr. Trump’s sudden announcement, according to a senior U.S. military official. Just last week, an official with U.S. and South Korean Combined Forces Command told reporters that the exercises would simulate combat against North Korean troops, who have gained crucial experience while fighting for Russia in its war against Ukraine.

Col. Ryan Donald, director of ​public affairs for the Combined Forces Command, United Nations Command and U.S. Forces Korea, said last Monday that ​the exercise reflected the changing character of war, including the growing use of unmanned systems, electronic warfare and cyberoperations.

“DPRK soldiers have deployed and fought in Ukraine, and they’ve taken those lessons they’ve learned ​there and brought them back to North Korea,” he said at a news conference in South Korea, as reported by The Associated Press. He was referring to North Korea’s official name, the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea.

“That changes the DPRK capability, and our training accounts for ⁠that threat,” he said.

The exercises are supposed to include 18,000 South Korean troops, as well as a number of U.S. troops who are already part of the 28,500 American service members stationed in South Korea.
